Puerto Cisnes is a coastal town in the Aysén Region, on the shores of the Puyuhuapi Channel. Fishing boats, a small harbor, and low-rise buildings stand beside wooded slopes. It is a stop for discovering everyday life in Chilean Patagonia, where settlements are closely connected to the water.

On journeys through the Patagonian channels, Puerto Cisnes may be included as a possible port of call. A walk along the waterfront and town streets offers a different experience from watching glaciers and remote fjords: here you see a lived-in corner of the coast. Whether the ship actually lands and how long it stays depend on sailing conditions and the cruise itinerary.

At Puerto Egas, the most interesting place to walk is right beside the water. On Santiago Island's western coast, black lava forms uneven ledges, small pools, and grottos. The surf alternately fills the hollows and exposes new stretches of rock. It is easy to spend a long time here watching crabs and other animals moving among the waves.

The coastal trail leads to grottos inhabited by Galápagos fur seals. These animals choose rocky places where they can shelter in the shade. Watching them becomes especially engaging when a seal raises its head, shifts position, or slips into the water. A guide helps distinguish fur seals from sea lions and point out details of their behavior.

The name Puerto Egas is associated with the owner of a company that mined salt on the island in the twentieth century. The inland route leads to an old salt crater, while the coastal route focuses on wildlife and rocky grottos. What you see depends on the trail chosen. The site suits those who love seascapes and are happy to stop and watch small movements at the water's edge.

## Puerto Escondido — a town of inviting beaches!

Puerto Escondido is one of the more densely populated towns in Mexico's Oaxaca State. It lies on the coast, 800 km south of Mexico City and 290 km from Oaxaca de Juárez, the state capital, stretching along a long coastal strip with around a dozen clean, welcoming beaches.

## Puerto Escondido — a surfer's paradise!

Avenida Pérez Gasga is the heart of the resort. It is home to numerous bars, hotels, cafés, restaurants, nightclubs, shops, and internet cafés. The resort is a paradise for surfers, with many beaches and colorful coves offering waves of different lengths and levels of difficulty. Alternatively, you can snorkel in a quiet lagoon and watch brightly colored fish, and, with luck, spot sea turtles and dolphins. Emerald and azure waters at a comfortable temperature, a fresh ocean breeze, green palms, and fine sand all create the feeling of arriving in a true tropical paradise.

Puerto Iguazú is in the north of Argentina, on the borders with Brazil and Paraguay. Iguazú National Park lies 18 km from the city. Visitors set out from here to see Iguazú Falls, situated near the borders with Brazil and Paraguay where the Iguazú River flows into the Paraná. Access to Iguazú National Park is via the Tancredo Neves Bridge (Tancredo Nevec Bridge), with wonderful views of the Iguazú River canyon. Walking through the park, you can see many species of orchids, birds, reptiles, and other plants and animals of the humid tropical forest. The viewing platforms bring you remarkably close to the power of nature and offer panoramas of the many waterfalls.

Beautiful landscapes open up before you, with waterfalls plunging 72 m into a gorge. The name “Iguazú” means “big water” in the language of the Guaraní people. Iguazú Falls lie on the border between Brazil's Paraná State and Argentina's Misiones Province. Both national parks are UNESCO World Heritage sites. Two-thirds of the cascades are on Argentine territory and one-third on the Brazilian side. To fully appreciate the falls' scale and power, it is worth seeing them from both countries. Yet even a walk across the many bridges over the Argentine side is breathtaking, with lush scenery, exotic birds, and butterflies. The structure of Iguazú Falls is extraordinary: a whole system of 272 two-tiered cascades forming a giant amphitheater, seemingly layered one above another. The border between Brazil and Argentina runs through the gorge of the main cascade, Garganta del Diablo, meaning “Devil's Throat.”

Several visitor routes have been created around the falls. One of the most memorable begins with a ride on an ecological train, followed by a walk to the Devil's Throat viewing platform. From here, there is a mesmerizing panorama of the most powerful cascade, carrying the greatest volume of water. The so-called Lower Circuit brings visitors closer to the cascades, with countless rainbows forming in the millions of droplets of spray. This area has a dock from which small motorboats set out on an exhilarating journey toward the walls of water. The Upper Circuit takes in the highest section of the falls, where the Iguazú cascades begin.

## Costa Rica's Caribbean coast

Puerto Limón is a hub of the Caribbean coast. Bananas and coffee are exported from here. Beautiful beaches, coconut palms, and azure waters offer everything you need for a wonderful break.

The beaches provide a full range of activities, from diving to windsurfing. Those seeking a more relaxed holiday can simply stretch out on the white sand or go deep-sea fishing.

Surfing, fishing, and excellent beaches! Rich coral reefs lie south of the city. Puerto Limón is a center of Afro-Caribbean culture in Costa Rica. The city is especially colorful during its carnival.
